A.biggest_strength: Interactive parameter customization allowing users to test custom client/server ISNs, variable payload sizes, random 32-bit numbers with modulo wraparound, and Wireshark-style relative numbering.
A.biggest_weakness: Poor mobile responsiveness: the sequence diagram has a rigid min-width of 480px, causing the entire server lifeline, server states, and arrowheads to be clipped off-screen at phone width.

B.biggest_strength: Brilliant visual mechanism that maps sequence numbers to individual byte stream blocks and internal TCB pointers (SND.NXT, RCV.NXT, SND.UNA), anchored by an intuitive, color-coordinated formula.
B.biggest_weakness: Fixed sequence numbers and payload: unlike Page A, users cannot input arbitrary custom ISNs or change payload lengths to experiment with different values.

structured_output.reasons: Page B is the clear winner for a networking class explainer. While Page A offers great input parameter customization, Page B visually demonstrates the actual mechanism of sequence and acknowledgment numbers using discrete byte blocks, animated sliding window pointers (SND.NXT, RCV.NXT, SND.UNA), and a beautifully color-coordinated formula (ack = seq + len + SYN + FIN). Furthermore, Page B provides exceptional depth (comparing against an actual Linux kernel loopback capture, explaining RFC 6528, 2·MSL realities, and TCP flags) and flawlessly reflows its SVG layout for mobile devices, whereas Page A's diagram cuts off the entire server side on mobile screens.
